name: Oural Green
lede: Oural Green is a pale, chalky yellow-green named with the French spelling of the Urals, the mountain range that marks the traditional line between Europe and Asia.

sections.title: A mountain range's name
sections.body:
The Ural Mountains run roughly north to south for about 2,500 kilometers through Russia and are conventionally treated as the boundary between the European and Asian continents, a convention rather than a geological fact [3]. Oural is the French spelling of Ural, consistent with how Maerz and Paul's 1930 dictionary borrowed several European place names in their French form [1]. Ridgway's 1912 standards plate this green on plate XVIII, hue 35 prime, tone f, and the ISCC-NBS dictionary of 1955 later filed the same swatch, block 135, as a light yellowish green, 3.9 units from that block's center [1]. Our library gives it the Munsell notation 6.7GY 8.7/2.5 [1].

Its nearest named neighbors are Pale Olivine, 3.8 units away, and Pale Veronese Green, 3.8 units away [1]. It sits in the same pale, chalky cluster as [[pale-olivine]] and [[tea-green]] [1].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: In our archive of 23,781 paintings, a color within six units of Oural Green covers at least five percent of the canvas in 65 works, a little over a quarter of one percent [2]. The earliest dated example is Antonello da Messina's 1475 Dead Christ supported by an angel, a floor and not a first, since the archive's early centuries are thin [2]. It peaks in the 1860s, in 6 of 926 paintings, three and a half times the archive's overall rate for that decade, and Vincent van Gogh carries it in three of his forty-nine paintings here, over twenty times the baseline rate [2]. Ninety-eight percent of its appearances sit in a painting's highlights rather than its mid-tones or shadows[2]. It shares a canvas with [[celadon]] far more than any other color word, over a hundred and fifty times the baseline[2]. These are photographs of aged, varnished paintings, read as screen colors, not pigment identifications[2].
